We need to propose a retrosynthesis route with 1 reaction for target SMILES: [CH2:1]=[C:2]([c:3]1[cH:4][cH:5][cH:6][cH:7][cH:8]1)[C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18]

Interpret: It's an alkene attached to phenyl, and a cyclopentanol with CF3? Actually C(F)(F)F attached to carbon 15? The SMILES: C=C(c1ccccc1)C1CCCC1C(O)C(F)(F)F? Wait need to convert: [CH2]=[C]([c1ccccc1])[C@@H]1[CH2][CH2][CH2][C@@]1(O)C(F)(F)F. That's a cyclopentanol with CF3 attached to carbon bearing OH? Actually C@@]1(O)C(F)(F)F means carbon 13 attached to OH and CF3? The carbon 13 is chiral, attached to OH and CF3? So product is a cyclopentanol with CF3 substituent.

The guidance: carbonyl-ene reaction retrosynthesis: break C=C and carbonyl to form C-C bond and OH. So forward reaction is carbonyl-ene: carbonyl + alkene -> allylic alcohol. In retrosynthesis, we need to break the C-O bond to get a carbonyl (ketone) and an alkene. So the precursor would be a ketone (maybe cyclopentanone with CF3) and an alkene (styrene). The carbonyl-ene forms the new C-C bond between the carbonyl carbon and the alkene's allylic carbon, generating a new C-O (hydroxyl) at the carbonyl oxygen? Actually ene reaction: carbonyl (C=O) + alkene -> allylic alcohol where the carbonyl oxygen becomes OH attached to the carbonyl carbon (now sp3). So the product has a hydroxyl on the carbon that was carbonyl carbon. So our target has OH on carbon 13 which is attached to CF3 and part of cyclopentane. So precursor likely cyclopentanone with CF3 at that carbon (i.e., 2,2,2-trifluoro-1-cyclopentanone?) Wait carbonyl carbon is attached to CF3? In product, carbon bearing OH also attached to CF3 and part of ring. So precursor would be carbonyl carbon attached to CF3 (i.e., trifluoroacetyl? Actually carbonyl carbon attached to CF3 would be CF3-CO-? That's trifluoroacetyl group, not part of ring. But here CF3 attached to same carbon as OH and ring, so carbonyl carbon is part of ring and has CF3 substituent. So precursor is a cyclopentanone with CF3 at the carbonyl carbon (i.e., 2,2,2-trifluoro-cyclopentanone). That carbonyl carbon is part of ring, attached to CF3 and two ring bonds. So precursor: O= C(C(F)(F)F) attached to ring. So structure: O=C1CCCC1C(F)(F)F? Actually carbonyl carbon is part of ring, so O=C1CCCC1C(F)(F)F? That would be a cyclopentanone with CF3 substituent at carbonyl carbon (makes it a gem-difluoro? Wait carbonyl carbon can't have CF3 and O simultaneously? Carbonyl carbon double bonded to O, single bond to CF3, and part of ring (two bonds). That's possible: trifluoromethyl ketone (CF3-CO-). But carbonyl carbon attached to CF3 and two ring carbons? That would be a quaternary carbon? Actually carbonyl carbon is sp2, attached to O (double), to CF3, and to two ring carbons? That's too many. So maybe CF3 attached to adjacent carbon, not carbonyl carbon. In product, carbon bearing OH also attached to CF3 and part of ring. So that carbon is sp3, attached to OH, CF3, and two ring bonds. In precursor, that carbon would be carbonyl carbon (C=O) attached to CF3 and two ring bonds. So yes carbonyl carbon attached to CF3 and two ring bonds, double bond to O. That's a trifluoromethyl ketone within ring (alpha-CF3 ketone). So precursor: O=C1CCCC1C(F)(F)F? That carbonyl carbon is part of ring, but the CF3 is attached to carbonyl carbon, which is also part of ring, making a 5-membered ring with carbonyl carbon as one member, and CF3 attached to it. That is possible: 2,2,2-trifluoro-cyclopentanone (CF3 at carbonyl carbon). SMILES: O=C1CCCC1C(F)(F)F? Let's test: O=C1CCCC1C(F)(F)F. That carbonyl carbon is part of ring (position 1). The CF3 attached to same carbon (makes carbonyl carbon have three substituents: O double, two ring bonds, CF3). That's four bonds (double counts as 2). So valence okay.

Now the other reactant is an alkene: styrene (C=C(c1ccccc1)H). Actually the product's alkene part is CH2= C(Ph)- attached to carbonyl carbon? In ene reaction, the alkene provides the allylic hydrogen that becomes attached to carbonyl oxygen? Wait product has CH2= C(Ph)- attached to carbon bearing OH? Actually product: CH2= C(Ph)- attached to carbon bearing OH? The product SMILES: CH2= C(Ph)-C(OH)(CF3)-cyclopentane? The CH2= C(Ph) is attached to the carbon bearing OH? Yes the carbon bearing OH is attached to the alkene carbon (the internal carbon). So in precursor, the alkene is CH2= C(Ph)-H? Actually the alkene carbon that bonds to carbonyl carbon is the internal carbon of alkene (C). So the alkene is CH2= C(Ph)-R? In product, R is the carbonyl carbon (now OH). So the alkene is CH2= C(Ph)-H (styrene). So precursor alkene is styrene (C= Cc1ccccc1). SMILES: C= Cc1ccccc1 (or C=CC1=CC=CC=C1?). Actually styrene is C=CC1=CC=CC=C1. That's CH2=CH-Ph. So yes.

Thus retrosynthesis: target -> apply reverse of carbonyl-ene: break C-O bond to give ketone (trifluoromethyl cyclopentanone) and alkene (styrene). That's one reaction.

We need template ID for carbonyl-ene. We saw template 1209837 earlier: retro_smarts_template: '[C:3]-[C:2](-[C:4])-[OH;D1;+0:1]>>C-C(=C)-C(=O)-[O;H0;D2;+0:1]-[C:2](-[C:3])-[C:4]'. This seems to be reverse of ene? It maps product with OH to reactants with carbonyl and alkene. So we can use that template.

We need to verify that applying template to target yields precursors. Let's try apply_template with target SMILES and template 1209837. Use correct SMILES format (no atom mapping). Target SMILES: C=C(c1ccccc1)C1CCCC1C(O)C(F)(F)F? Need to ensure correct stereochemistry not needed. Use: C=C(c1ccccc1)C1CCCC1C(O)C(F)(F)F. Let's test apply_template.
